text: This lab pulls together everything from this chapter into one real scenario. You're the technical architect asked to propose a fix, walking through table design, archiving, and CSDM governance together instead of as three separate problems.

A company has run ServiceNow in production for eight years. Its core Incident table has grown to 15 million records, and both list-view load times and scheduled reports have been quietly getting slower for two years. Twenty-three fields were added over the years by different project teams, nobody has ever archived a record, and every incident carries a relationship to a CMDB CI.

Per lesson 8, the first question is whether the table itself has gotten wider than it needs to be. Auditing the 23 added fields shows 14 are touched by fewer than 2 percent of incidents, mostly leftovers from retired integrations, while 9 are genuinely used across most incidents today. The recommendation: the 9 actively-used fields stay on the base table, and the 14 rarely-used fields move to a related extension table rather than being deleted, since a handful of old reports still reference them.

Per lesson 9, archive everything old isn't a real policy. This organization's confirmed compliance obligation requires incident records to remain available for three years after closure — nothing requires them to stay in the live table beyond that. The resulting policy: incidents closed more than three years ago move to an archive table on a recurring job, not deleted outright, while incidents closed within three years and all open incidents stay active.

This is the step lesson 10 makes necessary and that's easy to miss. Every archived incident still carries its CMDB relationship, but a CI's recent-incidents view, if it only queries the active table, will quietly stop showing anything older than three years — which can look like a CI had no problems rather than that its history was archived. The fix is to relabel CMDB-facing incident views to state their real time window, and document that rule so future CMDB reporting work doesn't reintroduce the same silent gap.

Narrower table, a specific three-year archiving policy, and relabeled CMDB views that own the consequence instead of hiding it — one documented plan, not three separate fixes. Next up: Chapter 4 begins, designing an enterprise integration strategy.
